data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories inevitably smuggles induction back into Popper's system because any decision to act on past test results presupposes the principle that the future will resemble the past, rendering the 'non-inductive' defense a semantic evasion.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If 'preference' can be decoupled entirely from expectations of future performance.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If there exists a non-inductive rationale for action that does not rely on uniformity.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'critical attitude' is sufficient to guide action without predictive power.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"While Popper formally denies that corroboration implies probability, the *act* of preferring one theory over another for practical application (e.g., building a bridge) functionally requires an inductive leap. If corroboration tells us nothing about the future, then preferring the corroborated theory is irrational unless one implicitly assumes nature's uniformity. The 'cost' of this view is admitting that Popper's epistemology fails to provide a complete foundation for scientific practice without borrowing from the very tradition he sought to overthrow.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
